Not exactly relevant but Waltz with Bashir could be considered. It’s an animated documentary that suddenly shifts to real footage of the aftermath of a massacre / genocide of Palestinians conducted by some lunatic Lebanese Christian’s enabled by the IDF.  It’s not so much a call to action but it suddenly jolts you with the weight of the true reality & scale of suffering experienced. 

Maybe films based on real events when at the end they show real footage of key moments that were in the film, e.g. City of God, or even show real footage years later, like Schindler’s List.

Have you seen Bamboozled also by Lee? The montage at the end is the best part of the movie, but besides that I would say it's just pretty good. Long ago Bert Williams was a black vaudeville star who used blackface, while subverting it, to have a career. He sung nobody, which was covered by Johnny cash. The film was made when gangsters were very popular in the black community. Lee is critical of the idea of keeping your dignity while using token stereotypes, even if it's done subversively. Dave Chappelle walked away from millions because he didn't like a laugh. He felt laughed at not laughed with. 

Ethnic Notions is the definitive film on blackface, but the montage is poetic.

"How To Blow Up A Pipeline" ends with a pretty literal call to action, telling the audience that there may be dire consequences to deciding to be an eco-terrorist and bombing polluters, but it's still a righteous work that must be done. It shows the spread of the group's manifesto as a hopeful victory.

Hilariously enough, Borat 2: Subsequent Movefilm. Same side of the political fence with a VASTLY different approach in every way. Baron Cohen purposefully brought the character back so that he could try to encourage people to vote a certain way in the 2020 election. The entire movie does that, but at the end it flat out says it with the text "Vote, or we will make execute."

Another one, although not necesarily a call to action but instead a point being made was the Fifth Estate, starring Benedict Cumberbatch as Julian Assange, the controversial founder of wikileaks. Cumberbatch, in character as Assange at the end of the film, lambasts the very idea of a movie adaptation, saying that audiences should instead come to their own conclusions, after which he turns and looks at the camera. Side note, I quite enjoy this movie despite it's critical lambasting.

Charlie Chaplin’s THE GREAT DICTATOR does this well. The whole film is a obvious criticism of Nazism and concludes with Chaplin’s character, who has been mistaken for The Führer, giving an impassioned speech about tolerance to a Naziesque crowd. The camera squares off with Chaplin so that he is speaking directly through its lens to the real world audience watching in the theater. That Chaplin’s character, who has been silent throughout the film, actually verbalizes his call to action to stand against intolerance makes the message that much more effective.

Walker by Alex Cox. Great film.

I don’t want to spoil it, just see it lol. I don’t normally give trigger warnings but this time just make sure you’re okay with graphic imagery. It’s very rooted in time and place but the overall sentiment is transcendental.

Wind River (2017) was written to raise awareness for missing and murdered indigenous women and ends with the quote: >!“While missing person statistics are compiled for every other demographic, none exist for Native American women.”!<

I don’t think it was misinterpreted at all. Blowing up one pipeline is ultimately also not going to make a dent in the climate apocalypse overall, but they were doing it as a clear statement of war. The manifesto is not about inspiring others to pull off similar feats. Remember, they were putting the exact same manifesto on SUVs they were just deflating the tires of at the beginning of the movie. They want to inspire people to take more direct response climate actions in their own backyards instead of just protesting or voting for the right government. So kids in Florida destroying yachts and threatening society to stop using those leisure vehicles? That’s a victory for their movement. If anyone in the audience want to risk going to jail by torching their local car dealership? That’s good too.

I think that ignores the twist, in that their plan is about making them  martyrs, bringing attention to the fact the petrochemical company gave that girl cancer. Their act of sabotage is in service of creating a compelling political statement. Blowing up day boats isn’t.

In Dear White People (2014), the film culminates with a black face party at the college where the film takes place. Then, over the end credits, they show pictures from real Black/Brown face parties at colleges across the country. Perhaps not a direct call to action, but it was a powerful demonstration of how “casual” or “jokey” racism is very much alive and well in the US.

I don't think the film was very interested in exploring 'the system'. The focus was entirely on this one individual and his Scrooge-esque reformation from charming scam artist to 'likeable rogue'. The film itself seemed totally smitten by him, and its criticism of wall st itself limited to a criticism of individuals' irresponsible behaviour rather than a fundamentally broken system.

Blue Bayou (2021), it's about a Korean-American adoptee but his parents never naturalized him so he's facing risk of deportation. 

From Wiki: As the film ends, real-life cases of other unnaturalized adoptees who are either facing deportation or have been deported are shown, along with the estimates by the Adoptee Rights Campaign of international adoptees who face similar circumstances.

Have you considered including a mention of *Starship Troopers*?   It ends directly asking you, the viewer, to sign up for the armed forces.  As a satire of propaganda films, this is of course, tongue-in-cheek, but maybe there is a place in your paper for that as an aside.

Interestingly, the film begins suggesting three options: Flight, Intelligence and Mobile Infantry (grunts, cannon fodder, etc.)  Then the the film slowly and subtly takes two of them off the table - the Pilots are shown to be stuck up jerks, the Intelligence job is shown to be soul-crushing, so by then end there's no question what you want to be:  MI!

That's a very bad reading of the ending imo. 

The point is that Belfort got off easy and is now doing the same grift, just legally. Look at the last shot of all the suckers looking eagerly at him, he's still the same con artist, but people still look up to him after all the things he did. It's basically shining a light on us the audience, and criticizing the American dream.

To be clear, I am in complete agreement with that interpretation of what the character is doing, but unfortunately I am not at all convinced that this is the film's intended reading. Or if it is the intended reading, I think it does a poor job of communicating that. The Scrooge narrative, the redemption arc, was such a spectacularly poor choice of narrative template if the intention was to be critical of the character in that epilogue.

I just don’t see how else you could interpret the final shot, to me, it seems very obvious. 

I never got a hint of any redemption arc. I'm really confused as to where you're getting a Scrooge narrative.

In the end of the movie he hits and rapes his wife, tries to take their child, and crashes a car with her in it. He goes to jail and says it's basically like summer camp. Then he gets out and is back to his same antics, with zero demonstration of any remorse. Where is the redemption?

I'm guessing you're not familiar with Scorsese's work if this is your takeaway.

The redemption arc is this: Belfort, presented as a charming but irresponsible rogue, lives a decadent lifestyle and loses everything because of it. I think you're misrepresenting the film if you took from it that the film doesn't show Belfort punished for his crimes. The film depicts his wife leaving him as the lowest point in his life, and we are made to sympathise with his realisation that he can't go on this way and needs to reform himself.

So after prison he re-styles himself as a business guru. To many viewers, both of us included, we can see that Belfort is a snake-oil salesman. But the film's attitude, as I see it, is that that lovable rogue Jordan Belfort has found a cheeky but otherwise socially meaningful use of talents he was previously putting to more destructive use.

Just like Dickens suggests that Britain would be better if more wealthy men like Scrooge had more humanity, but doesn't truly challenge the very concept of wealth, Scorsese suggests that Wall St would be better if more fraudsters like Belfort reigned in their excesses, and stops short at any deeper social critique.

The clincher for me was learning, only after watching the film, that the whole thing is an adaptation of the real Jordan Belfort's memoir. So no wonder that it comes across like Citizen Kane but if we were meant to like Kane at the end. (The real) Belfort and Scorsese are hyperfixated on individual behaviour and not on the system.

> The film's ending seems to want to suggest that Jordan Belafonte is now doing something positive with his business skills.

I'd completely disagree with that personally - it shows that far from giving up his old ways, Belfort has used his notoriety and infamy to become a common grifter who will continue to make money even if he can't lead the same life as before. In an era which seems to be filled with more tech grifters and fraudsters who are worshipped even though their wrongdoing is eventually exposed, it feels like an ending that has aged well.

I would argue that the film's tone is completely at odds with the way you see it. The film encourages us to see him as a lovable grifter. The ending hasn't aged well because it was obnoxious at the time: I refuse to see Belfort as this endearing rogue that the film seems to want to encourage me to. I would imagine that Belfort's memoir, which this film adapts, had a similar purpose.
